claim: The turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri) is the shortest-lived vertebrate with a thoroughly documented post-embryonic life.
source: The turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri) is the shortest-lived vertebrate with a thoroughly documented post-embryonic life, which, in the shortest-lived strains, amounts to four months (Cellerino et al., 2016; Hu and Brunet, 2018; Kim et al., 2016; Blazek, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: In the shortest-lived strains of turquoise killifish, lifespan amounts to four months.
source: The turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri) is the shortest-lived vertebrate with a thoroughly documented post-embryonic life, which, in the shortest-lived strains, amounts to four months (Cellerino et al., 2016; Hu and Brunet, 2018; Kim et al., 2016; Blazek, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Different wild turquoise killifish populations display differences in lifespan, both in the wild and in captivity.
source: At the same time, while sharing physiological adaptations that enable embryonic diapause and rapid sexual maturation, different wild turquoise killifish populations display differences in lifespan, both in the wild and in captivity (Terzibasi et al., 2008; Valenzano et al., 2015; Vrtílek et al., 2018), making this species an ideal evolutionary model to study the genetic basis underlying life history trait divergence within species.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Populations from arid regions exhibit the shortest lifespans, while populations from more semi-arid regions exhibit longer lifespans.
source: Characterization of life history traits in wild-derived laboratory strains of turquoise killifish revealed that while different populations have similar rates of sexual maturation (Blazek, 2017), populations from arid regions exhibit the shortest lifespans, while populations from more semi-arid regions exhibit longer lifespans (Blazek, 2017; Terzibasi et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Speed of sexual maturation and adult lifespan appear to be independent in turquoise killifish populations.
source: Hence, speed of sexual maturation and adult lifespan appear to be independent in turquoise killifish populations.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that different populations have similar rates of sexual maturation but different lifespans

claim: The improved reference genome assembly has a contig N50 of 7.8 kb.
source: We ran Allpaths-LG with all the available pair-end sequences, producing a combined assembly with a contig N50 of 7.8 kb, corresponding to a ~ 2 kb improvement from the previous versions.
evidence: Reported as a result of genome assembly analysis

claim: The improved reference genome assembly has a scaffold N50 of 1.5 Mb.
source: Two newly obtained 10X Genomics linked read libraries were used to correct and link scaffolds, resulting in a scaffold N50 of 1.5 Mb, that is a three-fold improvement from the best previous assembly.
evidence: Reported as a result of genome assembly analysis

claim: 92.2% of assembled bases were assigned to the 19 linkage groups.
source: With the improved continuity, we assigned 92.2% of assembled bases to the 19 linkage groups using two RAD-tag maps (Valenzano et al., 2015).
evidence: Reported as a result of genome assembly analysis

claim: Gene content assessment using the BUSCO method improved 'complete' BUSCOs from 91.43% and 94.59% to 95.20%.
source: Gene content assessment using the BUSCO method improved "complete" BUSCOs from 91.43% (Valenzano et al., 2015) and 94.59% (Reichwald et al., 2015) to 95.20%.
evidence: Reported as a result of genome assembly quality assessment

claim: The overall size of repeated regions is 1.003 Gb, accounting for 66% of the entire genome.
source: The overall size of repeated regions (masked regions) is 1.003 Gb, accounting for 66% of the entire genome, that is 20% higher than a previous estimate (Reichwald et al., 2009).
evidence: Reported as a result of genome assembly analysis

claim: Population GNP is located within the Gonarezhou National Park at high altitude and in an arid climate.
source: Population GNP is located within the Gonarezhou National Park at high altitude and in an arid climate (Koeppen-Geiger classification 'BWh', Figure 1—figure supplement 1), in a region at the outer edge of the turquoise killifish distribution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Dorn et al., 2011; Bartáková et al., 2013; Bartáková et al., 2015), which corresponds to the place of origin of the 'GRZ' laboratory strain, which has the shortest lifespan of all laboratory strains of turquoise killifish (Terzibasi et al., 2008; Valenzano et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations and climate classification data

claim: The 'GRZ' laboratory strain has the shortest lifespan of all laboratory strains of turquoise killifish.
source: Population GNP is located within the Gonarezhou National Park at high altitude and in an arid climate (Koeppen-Geiger classification 'BWh', Figure 1—figure supplement 1), in a region at the outer edge of the turquoise killifish distribution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Dorn et al., 2011; Bartáková et al., 2013; Bartáková et al., 2015), which corresponds to the place of origin of the 'GRZ' laboratory strain, which has the shortest lifespan of all laboratory strains of turquoise killifish (Terzibasi et al., 2008; Valenzano et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Genetic diversity (θWatterson) decreases from wet to dry population (GNP: 0.0011, NF414: 0.0036, NF303: 0.0072).
source: We found that π and θWatterson decrease from wet to dry population (θWatterson GNP: 0.0011, θWatterson NF414: 0.0036, θWatterson NF303: 0.0072; πGNP: 0.0009, πNF414: 0.0031, and πNF303: 0.0054).
evidence: Reported as a result of population genetic analysis

claim: Nucleotide diversity (π) decreases from wet to dry population (GNP: 0.0009, NF414: 0.0031, NF303: 0.0054).
source: We found that π and θWatterson decrease from wet to dry population (θWatterson GNP: 0.0011, θWatterson NF414: 0.0036, θWatterson NF303: 0.0072; πGNP: 0.0009, πNF414: 0.0031, and πNF303: 0.0054).
evidence: Reported as a result of population genetic analysis

claim: Dry populations have overall smaller genetic diversity than populations from less dry regions.
source: Hence, dry populations have overall smaller genetic diversity than populations from less dry regions.
evidence: Inferred from the calculated genetic diversity metrics

claim: The genetic differentiation between populations ranged between 0.14 and 0.26.
source: Overall, the genetic differentiation between populations ranged between 0.14 and 0.26 and was the highest between the more geographically distant population GNP (dry) and population NF303 (wet) (Figure 1a).
evidence: Reported as a result of FST analysis and shown in Figure 1a

claim: The genetic differentiation was highest between the more geographically distant population GNP (dry) and population NF303 (wet).
source: Overall, the genetic differentiation between populations ranged between 0.14 and 0.26 and was the highest between the more geographically distant population GNP (dry) and population NF303 (wet) (Figure 1a).
evidence: Reported as a result of FST analysis and shown in Figure 1a

claim: Population GNP (dry) experienced a strong population decline starting approximately 150 k generations ago.
source: The population GNP (dry) experienced a strong population decline starting approximately 150 k generations ago, a result consistent for both the sequenced individuals from the two sampling sites (GNP-G1-3 and GNP-G4, Figure 1a).
evidence: Inferred from PSMC analysis and shown in Figure 1a

claim: Population NF414 (intermediate) and NF303 (wet) show population expansion until recent time (~50 k generations ago).
source: Analysis of population NF414 (intermediate) (Figure 1a, NF414-Y and NF414-R) and NF303 (wet) (Figure 1a, blue line) shows population expansion until recent time (~50 k generations ago).
evidence: Inferred from PSMC analysis and shown in Figure 1a

claim: Effective population size (Ne) estimates are 107221.8, 338849.48 and 683693.25 for GNP, NF414 and NF303, respectively.
source: In line with the decrease in genetic diversity from wet to dry population, we found a decrease in Ne estimates (107221.8, 338849.48 and 683693.25 for GNP, NF414 and NF303, respectively; Figure 1b).
evidence: Calculated from genetic diversity data and shown in Figure 1b

claim: Dry populations from the outer edge of the species distribution show lower genetic diversity and smaller effective population size compared to population from intermediate and more wet regions.
source: Hence, our findings show that dry populations from the outer edge of the species distribution show lower genetic diversity and smaller effective population size compared to population from intermediate and more wet regions.
evidence: Summarizes findings from genetic diversity and effective population size analyses

claim: The strongest QTL for lifespan differences among long-lived and short-lived populations mapped on the sex chromosome.
source: The strongest QTL for lifespan differences among long-lived and short-lived populations mapped on the sex chromosome (Valenzano et al., 2015; Kirschner et al., 2012), in proximity to the sex determining locus (Valenzano et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published QTL studies

claim: The outlier approach did not reveal clear signatures of positive or purifying selection based on genetic differentiation in the four main chromosomal clusters associated with lifespan.
source: The outlier approach did not reveal clear signatures of positive or purifying selection based on genetic differentiation in the four main chromosomal clusters associated with lifespan in experimental strains of turquoise killifish (Figure 2).
evidence: Reported as a result of FST outlier analysis and shown in Figure 2

claim: The gene slc8a1 on chromosome 6 contains mutations with significant difference in allele frequencies between the wet and intermediate population.
source: The region on chromosome six includes the gene slc8a1, which contains mutations with significant difference in allele frequencies between the wet and intermediate population (Fisher's exact test implemented in PoPoolation; adjusted p value < 0.001).
evidence: Reported as a result of statistical testing of allele frequency differences

claim: All genes under the major FST peak on chromosome 10 showed significant difference in allele frequencies between the intermediate and wet population.
source: All genes under the major FST peak on chromosome 10 showed significant difference in allele frequencies between the intermediate and wet population (Fisher's exact test; adjusted p value < 0.001) and additionally, hibch had significantly different allele frequencies between the dry and wet population (Fisher's exact test; adjusted p value < 0.001).
evidence: Reported as a result of statistical testing of allele frequency differences

claim: hibch, lss and slc8a1 are differentially expressed between adult and old killifish.
source: Analyzing available turquoise killifish longitudinal RNA-Seq datasets generated in liver, brain and skin (Baumgart et al., 2017), we found that hibch, lss and slc8a1 are differentially expressed between adult and old killifish (Supplementary file 1J, adjusted p value < 0.01).
evidence: Reported as a result of RNA-Seq analysis from published data

claim: hibch is involved in amino acid metabolism.
source: hibch, lss and slc8a1 are involved in amino acid metabolism (Ferdinandusse et al., 2013), biosynthesis of cholesterol (Huff and Telford, 2005), and proton-mediated accelerated aging (Osanai et al., 2018), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: lss is involved in biosynthesis of cholesterol.
source: hibch, lss and slc8a1 are involved in amino acid metabolism (Ferdinandusse et al., 2013), biosynthesis of cholesterol (Huff and Telford, 2005), and proton-mediated accelerated aging (Osanai et al., 2018), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: slc8a1 is involved in proton-mediated accelerated aging.
source: hibch, lss and slc8a1 are involved in amino acid metabolism (Ferdinandusse et al., 2013), biosynthesis of cholesterol (Huff and Telford, 2005), and proton-mediated accelerated aging (Osanai et al., 2018), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: XM_015956265 (ZBTB14) is the only gene that is an FST outlier and that is differentially expressed in adult vs. old individuals between at least two populations in all tissues (liver, brain and skin).
source: Gene XM_015956265 (ZBTB14) is the only gene that is an FST outlier and that is differentially expressed in adult vs. old individuals between at least two populations in all tissues (liver, brain and skin).
evidence: Reported as a result of combined FST and differential expression analysis

claim: Two genomic regions with low genetic differentiation between all pairs of populations were found, suggesting strong purifying selection.
source: Based on the outlier approach, we found two genomic regions with low genetic differentiation between all pairs of populations, suggesting strong purifying selection.
evidence: Inferred from FST outlier analysis

claim: The first region under low genetic differentiation is located on the sex chromosome and contains the putative sex determining gene gdf6.
source: The first region is located on the sex chromosome and contains the putative sex determining gene gdf6 (Reichwald et al., 2015), which is hence conserved among these populations.
evidence: Reported as a result of FST outlier analysis with citation to published literature

claim: The sex chromosome region also contains sybu, a maternal-effect gene associated with the establishment of embryo polarity.
source: This same region also contains sybu, a maternal-effect gene associated with the establishment of embryo polarity (Nojima et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The second region under low genetic differentiation is located on chromosome nine and harbors the genes XM_015965812 (abi2-like), cnot11 and lcp1.
source: The second region under low genetic differentiation is located on chromosome nine and harbors the genes XM_015965812 (abi2-like), cnot11 and lcp1, which are involved in phagocytosis (Ulvila et al., 2011), mRNA degradation (Mauxion et al., 2013) and cell motility (Kell et al., 2018), respectively.
evidence: Reported as a result of FST outlier analysis with citations to published literature

claim: The structure of the turquoise killifish sex chromosome is compatible with a chromosomal translocation within an ancestral chromosome and a fusion event between two chromosomes.
source: We found that the structure of the turquoise killifish sex chromosome is compatible with a chromosomal translocation within an ancestral chromosome and a fusion event between two chromosomes.
evidence: Inferred from synteny analysis

claim: The translocation event within an ancestral chromosome corresponding to medaka's chromosome 16 and platyfish's linkage group three led to a repositioning of a chromosomal region containing the putative sex-determining gene gdf6.
source: The translocation event within an ancestral chromosome corresponding to medaka´s chromosome 16 and platyfish´s linkage group three led to a repositioning of a chromosomal region containing the putative sex-determining gene gdf6 (Figure 3b).
evidence: Inferred from synteny analysis and shown in Figure 3b

claim: The asymptotic McDonald-Kreitman α ranged from −0.21 to −0.01 in comparison to N. orthonotus.
source: The asymptotic McDonald-Kreitman α ranged from −0.21 to −0.01 in comparison to the very closely related sister species N. orthonotus, confirming limited genome-wide positive selection since divergence from N. orthonotus (Figure 4a).
evidence: Reported as a result of McDonald-Kreitman analysis and shown in Figure 4a

claim: Population GNP shows the lowest asymptotic McDonald-Kreitman α, as well as lower McDonald-Kreitman α values throughout all derived frequency bins.
source: The population GNP, located in an arid region at higher altitude and associated with the shortest recorded lifespan, shows the lowest asymptotic McDonald-Kreitman α, as well as lower McDonald-Kreitman α values throughout all derived frequency bins, potentially suggesting a higher load of slightly deleterious mutations segregating in this population (Figure 4a).
evidence: Reported as a result of McDonald-Kreitman analysis and shown in Figure 4a

claim: Using N. rachovii as an outgroup species, the asymptotic McDonald-Kreitman α ranged from −0.06 to 0.23 among populations.
source: Using as an outgroup species another annual killifish species, Nothobranchius rachovii (NRC), we confirmed the lowest asymptotic McDonald-Kreitman α value in the dry population GNP (Figure 4b). Additionally, using Nothobranchius rachovii (NRC) as outgroup species, the asymptotic McDonald-Kreitman α ranged from −0.06 to 0.23 among populations, indicating that more alleles were driven to fixation by positive selection in the ancestral lineage leading to Nothobranchius furzeri and Nothobranchius orthonotus.
evidence: Reported as a result of McDonald-Kreitman analysis and shown in Figure 4b

claim: More new mutations are assigned as the slightly deleterious category in the dry GNP population, compared to the other two populations.
source: Consistently with the overall lower McDonald-Kreitman α values throughout all derived frequency bins, we found more new mutations assigned as the slightly deleterious category in the dry GNP population, compared to the other two populations (indicated by the higher number of deleterious SNPs in proximity to 4NeS ~ 0 in the GNP population, Figure 4d, Supplementary file 1H).
evidence: Reported as a result of distribution of fitness effects analysis and shown in Figure 4d

claim: Populations with smaller effective population size have a higher proportion of new slightly deleterious variants, compared to larger populations.
source: Analyzing the distribution of fitness effect in these simulated populations, we confirmed that populations with smaller effective population size have a higher proportion of new slightly deleterious variants, compared to larger populations, which have relatively more newly arising gene variants that are highly deleterious, indicating that purifying selection in the large population is more efficient in removing mutations with deleterious effects.
evidence: Confirmed through simulation analysis using SLiM3

claim: The proportion of mutations causing a change in protein function is significantly larger in the GNP population compared to populations NF414 and NF303.
source: We found that the proportion of mutations causing a change in protein function is significantly larger in the GNP population compared to populations NF414 and NF303 (Chi-square test: PGNP-NF303 <1.87e-119, PGNP-NF414 <4.96e-57, PNF303-NF414< 3.51e-35, Figure 4e).
evidence: Reported as a result of statistical testing and shown in Figure 4e

claim: The mutations with predicted deleterious effects on protein function reached higher frequencies in the dry population GNP.
source: Additionally, the mutations with predicted deleterious effects on protein function reached also higher frequencies in the dry population GNP (Figure 4c).
evidence: Reported as a result of variant annotation analysis and shown in Figure 4c

claim: The dry population GNP had a significantly higher mean Consurf score for mutations at non-synonymous sites in frequency bins from 5–20% up to 40–60%, compared to populations NF414 and NF303.
source: We found that the dry population GNP had a significantly higher mean Consurf score for mutations at non-synonymous sites in frequency bins from 5–20% up to 40–60%, compared to populations NF414 (intermediate) and NF303 (wet) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Reported as a result of Consurf analysis and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The dry, short-lived population GNP has significantly more slightly deleterious mutations segregating in the population, compared to the populations NF414 and NF303.
source: Indeed, we found support to the hypothesis that the dry, short-lived population GNP has significantly more slightly deleterious mutations segregating in the population, compared to the populations NF414 and NF303 (Figure 5a, Median NOR: GNP: −0.17, NF414: −0.02, NF303: −0.01; Median NRC: GNP: −0.14, NF414: 0.00, NF303: 0.00; Wilcoxon rank sum test: NOR: PGNPNF303 <2.21e-105, PGNP-NF414 <1.19e-76, PNF303-NF414< 1.39e-06; NRC: PGNP-NF303 <4.61e-179, PGNP-NF414 <1.42e-100, PNF303-NF414< 5.96e-22), indicating that purifying selection is relaxed in GNP.
evidence: Reported as a result of direction of selection analysis with statistical testing and shown in Figure 5a

claim: There is a significant overrepresentation in the lower 2.5th DoS quantile in the GNP population for pathways associated with age-related diseases, including gastric cancer, breast cancer, neurodegenerative disease, mTOR signaling and WNT signaling.
source: We found a significant overrepresentation in the lower 2.5th DoS quantile (i.e. genes under relaxation of selection) in the GNP population for pathways associated with age-related diseases, including gastric cancer, breast cancer, neurodegenerative disease, mTOR signaling and WNT signaling (q-value <0.05, Figure 5b, Supplementary file 1I).
evidence: Reported as a result of pathway overrepresentation analysis and shown in Figure 5b

claim: There is a significant enrichment for mitochondrial pathways in population NF303 in genes within the upper 2.5th DoS values.
source: Analyzing the pathways affected by genes within the upper 2.5th DoS values – corresponding to genes undergoing adaptive evolution – we found a significant enrichment for mitochondrial pathways – potentially compensatory (Cui et al., 2019) – in population NF303 (Figure 5b, Supplementary file 1I).
evidence: Reported as a result of pathway overrepresentation analysis and shown in Figure 5b

claim: Differences in effective population size among wild turquoise killifish are associated with an extensive relaxation of purifying selection, significantly affecting genes involved in age-related diseases.
source: Overall, our results show that differences in effective population size among wild turquoise killifish are associated with an extensive relaxation of purifying selection, significantly affecting genes involved in age-related diseases, and which could have cumulatively contributed to reducing individual survival.
evidence: Summarizes findings from multiple analyses

claim: The turquoise killifish sex chromosome appears to have evolved through two independent chromosomal events, that is a translocation and a fusion event.
source: Using the new turquoise killifish genome assembly and synteny analysis with medaka and platyfish, we reconstructed the origin of the turquoise killifish sex chromosome, which appears to have evolved through two independent chromosomal events, that is a translocation and a fusion event.
evidence: Inferred from synteny analysis

claim: Strong purifying selection maintains low genetic diversity among populations at genomic regions underlying key species-specific traits, such as in proximity to the sex-determining region.
source: While we found that strong purifying selection maintains low genetic diversity among populations at genomic regions underlying key species-specific traits, such as in proximity to the sex-determining region, demography and genetic drift largely shape genome evolution, leading to relaxation of selection and the accumulation of deleterious mutations.
evidence: Inferred from FST outlier analysis and genetic diversity patterns

claim: Demography and genetic drift largely shape genome evolution, leading to relaxation of selection and the accumulation of deleterious mutations.
source: While we found that strong purifying selection maintains low genetic diversity among populations at genomic regions underlying key species-specific traits, such as in proximity to the sex-determining region, demography and genetic drift largely shape genome evolution, leading to relaxation of selection and the accumulation of deleterious mutations.
evidence: Inferred from multiple population genetic analyses

claim: Isolated populations from an arid region, dwelling at higher altitude and characterized by shorter lifespan, experienced extensive population bottlenecking and a sharp decline in effective population size.
source: We showed that isolated populations from an arid region, dwelling at higher altitude and characterized by shorter lifespan, experienced extensive population bottlenecking and a sharp decline in effective population size.
evidence: Inferred from PSMC analysis and effective population size estimates

claim: Relaxation of selection in more drifted populations significantly affected the accumulation of deleterious gene variants in pathways associated with neurodegenerative diseases and WNT-signaling.
source: We found that relaxation of selection in more drifted populations significantly affected the accumulation of deleterious gene variants in pathways associated with neurodegenerative diseases and WNT-signaling (Figure 5).
evidence: Reported as a result of pathway overrepresentation analysis and shown in Figure 5

claim: The complex genetic architecture of lifespan differences among killifish populations is entirely compatible with genome-wide relaxation of selection.
source: While simple traits, such as male tail color and sex have a simple genetic architecture among turquoise killifish populations (Valenzano et al., 2015; Valenzano et al., 2009), we find that the complex genetic architecture of lifespan differences among killifish populations (Valenzano et al., 2015) is entirely compatible with genome-wide relaxation of selection.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of positive selection signatures at QTL regions and genome-wide patterns of relaxed selection

claim: The absence of genomic signature of positive selection in genomic regions underlying survival QTL in killifish suggest that the neutral accumulation of deleterious mutations may be the evolutionary mechanism underlying survival differences among turquoise killifish populations.
source: Additionally, the absence of genomic signature of positive selection in genomic regions underlying survival QTL in killifish suggest that, rather than directional selection, the neutral accumulation of deleterious mutations may be the evolutionary mechanism underlying survival differences among turquoise killifish populations, in line with the mutation accumulation theory of aging.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of positive selection signatures at QTL regions

claim: The uncoupling of age of sexual maturation from adult lifespan in different turquoise killifish populations is more compatible with the mutation accumulation theory of aging.
source: However, different wild populations of turquoise killifish have similar time to sexual maturation and yet different lifespan (Blazek, 2017). Hence, the uncoupling of age of sexual maturation from adult lifespan in different turquoise killifish populations is more compatible with the mutation accumulation theory of aging.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that sexual maturation and lifespan are uncoupled, combined with citation to published data

claim: Historical fluctuations in the size of natural turquoise killifish populations, especially in isolated populations living in more arid and elevated habitats, weakened the strength of natural selection, ultimately contributing to increased load of deleterious gene variants.
source: However, historical fluctuations in the size of natural turquoise killifish populations, especially in isolated populations living in more arid and elevated habitats, weakened the strength of natural selection, ultimately contributing to increased load of deleterious gene variants, preferentially in genes associated with aging-related diseases and in the WNT pathway.
evidence: Inferred from demographic history, distribution of fitness effects, and pathway enrichment analyses

claim: Small effective population size leads to the accumulation of aging-causing mutations that together contribute to the genetic architecture of lifespan.
source: We hypothesize that small effective population size leads to the accumulation of aging-causing mutations that together contribute to the genetic architecture of lifespan.
evidence: Proposed as a hypothesis based on the study findings

claim: Short-lived populations from the outer margin of the species range have small population size and accumulate deleterious mutations in genes significantly enriched in the WNT signaling pathway, neurodegeneration, cancer and the mTOR pathway.
source: Short-lived populations from the outer margin of the species range have small population size and accumulate deleterious mutations in genes significantly enriched in the WNT signaling pathway, neurodegeneration, cancer and the mTOR pathway.
evidence: Summarizes findings from effective population size estimates, distribution of fitness effects, and pathway enrichment analyses

claim: Limited population size due to habitat fragmentation and repeated population bottlenecks, by increasing the genome-wide mutation load, exacerbates the effects of mutation accumulation and cumulatively contribute to the short adult lifespan.
source: We propose that limited population size due to habitat fragmentation and repeated population bottlenecks, by increasing the genome-wide mutation load, exacerbates the effects of mutation accumulation and cumulatively contribute to the short adult lifespan.
evidence: Proposed as a conclusion based on the study findings

claim: Variations in population size among natural populations is expected to affect the rate of accumulation of advantageous and slightly deleterious gene variants.
source: Variations in population size among natural populations is expected to affect the rate of accumulation of advantageous and slightly deleterious gene variants, hence impacting the relative contribution of selection and drift to genetic polymorphisms (Lanfear et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Populations living in fragmented habitats, subjected to continuous and severe bottlenecks, are expected to undergo dramatic population size reduction and drift.
source: Populations living in fragmented habitats, subjected to continuous and severe bottlenecks, are expected to undergo dramatic population size reduction and drift, which can significantly impact the accumulation of genetic polymorphisms in genes affecting important life history traits (Nonaka et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The mutation accumulation theory of aging attributes the evolution of aging to germline-encoded genetic variants accumulating in populations due to the age-dependent weakening of purifying selection.
source: The mutation accumulation theory of aging (MA) attributes the evolution of aging to germline-encoded genetic variants accumulating in populations due to the age-dependent weakening of purifying selection, which becomes less efficient to remove from the gene pool gene variants that negatively impact fitness in late life (Charlesworth, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The antagonistic pleiotropy theory of aging states that positive selection could favor gene variants that, while overall beneficial for individual fitness, may have detrimental effects in late life.
source: The antagonistic pleiotropy (AP) theory of aging, instead, states that positive selection could favor gene variants that, while overall beneficial for individual fitness, may have detrimental effects in late life (Charlesworth, 2000; Williams, 1957).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Aging-determining gene variants occurring due to mutation accumulation evolve as nearly-neutral variants.
source: In fact, while aging-determining gene variants occurring due to mutation accumulation evolve as nearly-neutral variants, aging-determining gene variants emerging via antagonistic pleiotropism evolve as positive selected variants.
evidence: Based on established evolutionary theory

claim: Aging-determining gene variants emerging via antagonistic pleiotropism evolve as positive selected variants.
source: In fact, while aging-determining gene variants occurring due to mutation accumulation evolve as nearly-neutral variants, aging-determining gene variants emerging via antagonistic pleiotropism evolve as positive selected variants.
evidence: Based on established evolutionary theory

claim: Killifish repeatedly and independently colonized highly fragmented habitats, characterized by cycles of rainfalls and drought.
source: Among vertebrates, killifish represent a unique system, as they repeatedly and independently colonized highly fragmented habitats, characterized by cycles of rainfalls and drought (Furness, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Intermittent precipitation and periodic drought pose strong selective pressures leading to the evolution of embryonic diapause in killifish.
source: While on the one hand intermittent precipitation and periodic drought pose strong selective pressures leading to the evolution of embryonic diapause, an adaptation that enables killifish to survive in absence of water (Cellerino et al., 2016; Hu and Brunet, 2018), on the other hand they cause habitat and population fragmentation, promoting inbreeding and genetic drift.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Intermittent precipitation and periodic drought cause habitat and population fragmentation, promoting inbreeding and genetic drift in killifish.
source: While on the one hand intermittent precipitation and periodic drought pose strong selective pressures leading to the evolution of embryonic diapause, an adaptation that enables killifish to survive in absence of water (Cellerino et al., 2016; Hu and Brunet, 2018), on the other hand they cause habitat and population fragmentation, promoting inbreeding and genetic drift.
evidence: Inferred from ecological conditions and their expected evolutionary consequences

claim: Turquoise killifish has emerged as a powerful new laboratory model to study experimental biology of aging due to its short lifespan and wide range of aging-related changes.
source: Turquoise killifish has recently emerged as a powerful new laboratory model to study experimental biology of aging due to its short lifespan and to its wide range of aging-related changes, which include neoplasias (Di Cicco et al., 2011), decreased regenerative capacity (Wendler et al., 2015), cellular senescence (Ahuja et al., 2019; Valenzano et al., 2006), and loss of microbial diversity (Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Aging-related changes in turquoise killifish include neoplasias, decreased regenerative capacity, cellular senescence, and loss of microbial diversity.
source: Turquoise killifish has recently emerged as a powerful new laboratory model to study experimental biology of aging due to its short lifespan and to its wide range of aging-related changes, which include neoplasias (Di Cicco et al., 2011), decreased regenerative capacity (Wendler et al., 2015), cellular senescence (Ahuja et al., 2019; Valenzano et al., 2006), and loss of microbial diversity (Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Adult survival has a complex genetic architecture in turquoise killifish.
source: Mapping genetic loci associated with lifespan differences among turquoise killifish populations showed that adult survival has a complex genetic architecture (Valenzano et al., 2015; Kirschner et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published QTL studies
